content: Uterine prolapse occurs when the uterus descends from its normal position in the pelvic cavity into the vaginal canal. This condition can lead to a variety of symptoms, causes, and treatment options, which are detailed below. Symptoms of Uterine Prolapse: A sensation of sitting on a small ball. Difficulty or pain during sexual intercourse. Frequent urination or a sudden, urgent need to empty the bladder. Persistent low backache. Pain during intercourse. Protrusion of the uterus and cervix through the vaginal opening. Recurrent bladder infections. A feeling of heaviness or pulling in the pelvic region. Vaginal bleeding or an increase in vaginal discharge. Symptoms often worsen when standing or sitting for extended periods. Causes of Uterine Prolapse: The uterus is supported in the pelvis by muscles, ligaments, and connective tissues. Uterine prolapse occurs when these structures weaken, allowing the uterus to descend into the vaginal canal. Risk Factors: Women who have had one or more vaginal births are at higher risk. Aging and reduced estrogen levels after menopause can contribute to uterine prolapse. Chronic coughing and obesity increase pressure on the pelvic floor, exacerbating the condition. Rarely, a pelvic tumor can cause uterine prolapse. Chronic constipation and straining during bowel movements can worsen the condition. When to Seek Medical Care: If you experience symptoms of uterine prolapse, it is important to schedule an appointment with your healthcare provider. Diagnosis: A pelvic examination performed while the patient bears down (as if pushing during childbirth) can reveal the extent of uterine descent: Mild prolapse: The cervix drops into the lower part of the vagina. Moderate prolapse: The cervix protrudes out of the vaginal opening. The exam may also identify other conditions, such as: Cystocele: Protrusion of the bladder and the front vaginal wall into the vaginal area. Rectocele: Protrusion of the rectum and the back vaginal wall into the vaginal area. Lower positioning of the urethra and bladder in the pelvis. Rarely, a pelvic tumor causing the prolapse. Treatment Options: Treatment is not always necessary unless symptoms are bothersome. Most women seek treatment when the uterus descends to the vaginal opening. Treatment options include: Vaginal Pessary: A vaginal pessary is a rubber or plastic device, often donut-shaped, inserted into the vagina to support the uterus. It can be a temporary or permanent solution. Pessaries are custom-fitted for each woman, and some resemble a diaphragm used for birth control. Many women can learn to insert, clean, and remove the pessary themselves. Pessaries may cause irritation, abnormal-smelling discharge, or damage to the vaginal wall (mucosa). They require regular cleaning, sometimes performed by a healthcare provider. Some pessaries may interfere with sexual intercourse by limiting penetration depth. Lifestyle Changes: Weight loss is recommended for obese women with uterine prolapse. Avoid heavy lifting or straining, as these activities can worsen symptoms. Chronic coughing should be treated or prevented, as it can exacerbate symptoms. Smoking cessation is advised if coughing is related to smoking. Surgery: Surgery is considered when prolapse symptoms outweigh the risks of surgical intervention. The type of surgery depends on factors such as: Degree of prolapse. Desire for future pregnancies. Other medical conditions. The woman’s preference to retain vaginal function. Age and general health. Some procedures, like sacrospinous fixation, support the uterus using nearby ligaments without removing it. Vaginal hysterectomy is often performed to correct uterine prolapse. Any associated sagging of the vaginal walls, urethra, bladder, or rectum can be surgically corrected simultaneously. Prognosis: Women with mild uterine prolapse often do not experience bothersome symptoms and may not require treatment. Vaginal pessaries are effective for many women. Surgery typically provides excellent results, though some women may require additional treatment in the future. Possible Complications: Severe cases of uterine prolapse may lead to ulceration and infection of the cervix and vaginal walls. Cystocele can result in urinary tract infections and other urinary symptoms. Rectocele can cause constipation and hemorrhoids. Prevention: Strengthening pelvic floor muscles through Kegel exercises can reduce the risk of uterine prolapse. Postmenopausal women may benefit from estrogen therapy (vaginal or oral) to maintain connective tissue and muscle tone.
